stories.title: Logos Faith Tests Modular Construction for Affordable Housing Scale
stories.excerpt: Pastor Martin Porter, courtesy of Logos Faith Since its launch in 2017, Los Angeles-based Logos Faith Development has worked with religious institutions throughout Southern California to convert underutilized land into affordable housing units. The nonprofit organization uses property tax-exempt developments to attract developers and investors to projects that might otherwise be difficult to finance. The developer’s pipeline is currently valued at approximately $750 million and consists of more than 2,000 affordable housing units being developed in partnership with up to 30 faith-based organizations. The organization aims to break ground on five projects annually through 2028. Now, Logos Faith is determining whether modular construction can help achieve those goals more quickly and efficiently. The organization has partnered with Model/Z to test the build type at the Logos-Grant Housing Apartments, located at 105th Street and Central Avenue in South Los Angeles. “We decided to enter the fray with this project to learn by doing,” Logos Faith’s Partner and Founder, Pastor Martin Porter, told Connect CRE. “We want to evaluate modular to see if it makes sense to deploy this build type on more of our projects.” Testing a Different Approach For now, Logos Faith relies more heavily on traditional stick-built construction than on modular construction. The company has completed the 71-unit Casa Paloma in Orange County and the 49-unit Silver Star Apartments in Los Angeles. It also recently broke ground on the 138-unit St. Rest Community in Los Angeles. Modular construction differs from traditional stick builds in that individual sections of an apartment building are manufactured in a controlled factory environment. The completed modules are then transported to the development site and assembled. bullets: Logos Faith Development testing modular construction at South Los Angeles project with Model/Z partner.
$750M pipeline of 2,000+ affordable units across 30 faith-based organizations through 2028.

stories.summary: Logos Faith Development, a LA-based nonprofit, is piloting modular construction at Logos-Grant Housing Apartments in South LA to determine if the build type can accelerate its $750 million pipeline of 2,000+ affordable units developed with faith-based institutions. The organization aims to break ground on five projects per year through 2028 and sees modular as a potential lever to meet that cadence. Tax-exempt financing and nonprofit structure have enabled deal completion where conventional financing fails.
stories.impact: If modular proves cost and schedule-efficient for affordable multifamily in LA, it could unlock faster delivery and lower per-unit costs in a market with severe housing shortages, validating the model for replication across other nonprofits and mixed-income developers. Success here signals permitting/zoning acceptance for modular in LA County, reducing execution risk for future adaptive-reuse and ground-up affordable projects.

stories.title: Watermark Capital Moves Forward With School-to-Resi Conversion in Crown Heights
stories.excerpt: The 42-unit residential conversion of a former Roman Catholic school at 560 Sterling Place in Crown Heights, Brooklyn, is well underway. Watermark Capital Group’s redevelopment project at the corner of Classon Avenue and Sterling Place is going ahead at a former school campus owned by its neighbor, St. Teresa of Avila Roman Catholic Church. Site plans addressed to 783 Classon Avenue, which shares a tax lot with 560 Sterling Place, were filed Thursday with New York City’s Department of Buildings. The filing details the vertical expansion of an existing building to include a 42,181-square-foot residence and a 57,449-square-foot community facility. Signatories for the recent permits tie ownership to the Catholic Church and Watermark. Watermark, through the entity 560 Sterling, previously obtained the site’s ground lease from St. Teresa of Avila, according to a memorandum of lease filed Tuesday. The document references an initial lease signed in April 2024 and later modified in June 2025. The Tuesday filing coincided with a $16.48 million construction loan for the leasehold provided to Watermark’s project by California-based lender Genesis Capital. Wolfe Landau, a founding partner at Watermark, signed for the developer on the memorandum of lease and the loan agreement. The developer’s office did not respond to requests for comment. St. Teresa of Avila’s former school campus, which spans Classon Avenue between Sterling Place and St. Johns Place was once home to Brooklyn Jesuit Prep Middle School. The school relocated to East Flatbush in 2020. The remaining campus buildings are now leased to the New York State Court Officers Academy, which lists its offices at 541 St. Johns Place. St. Teresa of Avila leaders announced in June 2025 that its own church at 563 Sterling Place would be closing its doors, citing financial strain, declining participation and a deferred, multimillion-dollar repair bill. bullets: Watermark Capital converting former Catholic school to 42-unit residential at 560 Sterling Place, Crown Heights.
$16.48M construction loan secured; ground lease from St. Teresa of Avila Church filed June 2025.
42,181 SF residential + 57,449 SF community facility; permits filed with NYC DOB.
stories.summary: Watermark Capital is advancing a 42-unit residential conversion of a former Catholic school campus at 560 Sterling Place in Brooklyn's Crown Heights, with site plans and a $16.48 million construction loan filed in recent weeks. The project includes a community facility component and operates under a ground lease from the adjacent St. Teresa of Avila Church, filed in June 2025. Permits were filed with NYC's Department of Buildings in the past week.
stories.impact: Successful school-to-resi conversions in Brooklyn create a replicable playbook and attract capital to underutilized institutional real estate, especially in supply-constrained submarkets like Crown Heights. The ground-lease structure with a religious anchor reduces acquisition risk and enables creative financing, signaling a viable path for developers seeking tax-exempt and community-use leverage in expensive urban neighborhoods.

stories.title: Japanese Firm Orix Provides $55M Refi for 200-Unit Seattle Apartment Complex
stories.excerpt: A joint venture among Mack Real Estate Group, Silverstein Properties and Cantor Fitzgerald has secured $55 million to refinance Swell Apartments, a 200-unit multifamily complex in Downtown Seattle, Wash., Commercial Observer can first report. Japanese investment firm Orix Real Estate Capital provided the debt, while Newmark’s Jordan Roeschlaub, Chris Kramer, Sam Speciale and Lance Tillman arranged the transaction. Located at 821 South Washington Street in the Yesler Terrace neighborhood of Seattle’s Chinatown-International District, Swell Apartments opened in 2024. The building features a rooftop sky lounge, a fitness center, coworking spaces and private parking. Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Orix Real Estate Capital provides $55M refi for 200-unit Swell Apartments, Downtown Seattle, opened 2024.
JV of Mack Real Estate, Silverstein Properties, Cantor Fitzgerald; asset in Yesler Terrace/Chinatown-ID.
Early refi one year post-opening signals strong operational performance and lender confidence in Seattle market.
stories.summary: A joint venture among Mack Real Estate Group, Silverstein Properties, and Cantor Fitzgerald has secured a $55 million refinance from Japanese investor Orix Real Estate Capital for Swell Apartments, a 200-unit multifamily complex in Downtown Seattle's Yesler Terrace neighborhood that delivered in 2024. The early refi, just one year into operations, suggests strong leasing velocity and operational metrics. Newmark arranged the transaction.
stories.impact: Early refinance availability at attractive terms for a new Seattle multifamily asset signals resilient demand and pricing power in Downtown Seattle, particularly in the Chinatown-International District submarket. This validates recent delivery as cash-flowing and refinanceable, lowering developer execution risk and likely spurring additional ground-up multifamily starts in the neighborhood.

stories.title: Diptyque Signs Full-Floor Lease in North American Headquarters Move
stories.excerpt: George Comfort & Sons and building owner Wohio Holding Inc. announced a new lease agreement with Diptyque at 16 East 34th St., a newly renovated office and retail building located between Madison and Fifth Avenues in Murray Hill. Diptyque will occupy 18,017 square feet in a full-floor lease for its North American headquarters. As part of a 10-year lease, the global luxury brand, known for its perfumes, skincare and home decor, will more than double its current 8,097-square-foot footprint when it moves from 240-246 West 35th Street in the first quarter of 2027. “As a brand defined by style and luxury, Diptyque’s decision to make 16 East 34th Street its North American headquarters speaks to the tower’s high-end design and hands-on management and service,” said GC&S Peter Duncan. “The reimagined lobby and inspiring roof deck are valued enhancements that continue to draw the city’s top companies.” Ownership was represented in the lease transaction by George Comfort & Sons’ Duncan, Alexander Bermingham and James Donaldson. Diptyque was represented by Laurence Carroll of Cushman & Wakefield. The post Diptyque Signs Full-Floor Lease in North American Headquarters Move appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Diptyque luxury brand relocates North American HQ to 16 East 34th St., Manhattan (Murray Hill).
Full-floor lease of 18,017 SF; more than doubles current 8,097 SF footprint; moves Q1 2027.
10-year lease signals confidence in Manhattan office market; trophy building class commands premium rents.
stories.summary: Luxury fashion brand Diptyque has signed a 10-year, full-floor lease for 18,017 square feet at the newly renovated 16 East 34th Street in Manhattan's Murray Hill, more than doubling its current footprint at 240-246 West 35th Street. The relocation is set for Q1 2027. George Comfort & Sons represented the landlord, Wohio Holding Inc., while Cushman & Wakefield represented Diptyque.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily. However, this trophy-class office move signals ongoing corporate HQ consolidation in luxury Manhattan buildings, which can pressurize Class-A office availability and sustain high-end office rents in places like Murray Hill, subtly affecting white-collar job density and demand for premium rental apartments in that submarket.

stories.title: Jay Roberts of Prosper Group: 5 Questions

The CEO of Miami-based Prosper Group recently closed on a $50 million site along the Miami River in the city’s Brickell district. The 1-acre site includes 66 Southwest Sixth Street and 625 Southwest First Avenue, along with about 300 feet of river frontage. Before he embarked on a career as a real estate developer, Roberts worked on Wall Street. Among the large deals he worked on was the $2.6 billion initial public offering of Paramount Group Real Estate Investment Trust. As he builds his real estate portfolio, Roberts also is curating a social media following through his podcast, “The Long Game,” and his 187,000 followers on Instagram. The following conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: You’re pretty new to South Florida. What are you working on? We’re not looking to bite off more than we can chew, and we just want to execute what’s in front of us. We just closed on a site on the Miami River for $50 million to build a luxury high-rise, and then we have a second commercial building coming that we haven’t announced, but it’s a two-phase project. We’re looking for the cream-of-the-crop sites. My background is investment banking and finance. I worked on Wall Street at Bank of America Merrill Lynch. I moved to Miami and there was so much real estate development happening here. I met a developer, Dan Kodsi, in 2019. bullets: Prosper Group CEO Jay Roberts closed $50M site in Miami Brickell along Miami River.
1-acre site at 66 SW 6th St. and 625 SW 1st Ave.; includes 300 feet river frontage.
$2.8B pipeline: three Miami, one Tampa project; focus on waterfront, best-in-class sites.
stories.summary: Jay Roberts' Miami-based Prosper Group has closed a $50 million acquisition of a 1-acre waterfront site in the Brickell district along the Miami River, including 300 feet of riverfront. Roberts, formerly on Wall Street, now maintains a $2.8 billion development pipeline of three projects in Miami and one in Tampa, focused on waterfront and best-in-class sites. The firm aims to execute deliberately rather than overextend.
stories.impact: Miami Brickell waterfront acquisitions at scale signal sustained capital inflow into luxury multifamily development in Miami's highest-barrier submarket. The $2.8B pipeline and focus on river-fronting assets may drive up land costs in Brickell and underscore strength in trophy multifamily demand, setting pricing benchmarks for competing developers and likely accelerating density/height in the neighborhood.

stories.title: MMCC Arranges Financing for Orange Multifamily Acquisition
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap Capital Corporation (MMCC) arranged $12.6 million in financing for the acquisition of Bel Air and El Commodor Apartments, two contiguous 27-unit multifamily properties located at 315-343 S. Bedford Rd. in Orange. Rick Judge, senior managing director in MMCC’s Orange County office, secured the financing on behalf of a private client. The loan was provided by a national bridge lender and features a two-year term with full-term interest only payments and an 80% loan-to-value ratio. “This financing provides the borrower with a flexible bridge structure to execute its business plan for two well-located multifamily assets,” said Judge. “The properties’ proximity to major healthcare employers, the MainPlace Mall and regional transportation corridors supports their long-term investment profile.” Bel Air and El Commodor Apartments offer studio, one- and two-bedroom units within gated communities featuring courtyards. The properties are situated approximately half a mile from the multi-phase redevelopment of MainPlace Mall and within walking distance of Children’s Hospital of Orange County and Providence St. Joseph Hospital. The post MMCC Arranges Financing for Orange Multifamily Acquisition appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: MMCC arranged $12.6M bridge financing for 54-unit multifamily acquisition in Orange, CA.
Bel Air and El Commodor Apartments; two-year bridge, 80% LTV, interest-only payments.

stories.summary: Marcus & Millichap Capital Corporation arranged $12.6 million in bridge financing for the acquisition of Bel Air and El Commodor Apartments, two contiguous 27-unit properties totaling 54 units at 315-343 S. Bedford Road in Orange, California. The loan carries a two-year term with full interest-only payments and 80% LTV from a national bridge lender. The properties are located near the MainPlace Mall redevelopment and major healthcare employers.
stories.impact: Bridge financing availability for smaller multifamily value-add in Orange County (near healthcare anchors and retail redevelopment) signals operational confidence and refinance-ability, encouraging smaller sponsors and investors to acquire workforce housing near employment nodes. MainPlace Mall redevelopment as a nearby catalyst improves long-term lease-up and rent growth prospects, making acquisition of stabilized-but-aging stock attractive.

stories.title: RFR Buys Prada-Anchored Upper East Side Retail Condo at 841 Madison Avenue for $57M
stories.excerpt: An Upper East Side retail condominium at 841 Madison Avenue has traded hands for $57 million, Commercial Observer has learned. JSRE Acquisitions, which is associated with the Safra family and Status Capital, sold the East 70th Street unit occupied by luxury fashion house Prada to Aby Rosen and Michael Fuchs‘s RFR Holding, according to the brokers. Global Advisory founder Ross Mezzo and Ezra Saffati from Majestic Acquisitions represented the buyer and the seller. “This sale is a clear signal that Madison Avenue has fully reclaimed its position as a premier luxury retail corridor in Manhattan. With Prada anchoring this retail condo, we’re seeing exactly the kind of high-caliber tenancy that’s driven rents up and quality up across Madison Avenue over the past 18 months,” Mezzo said in a statement to CO. It’s unclear when JSRE acquired the property and what the value of that transaction was, but the retail unit traded for $51 million to Ashkenazy Acquisitions in 2010, The Real Deal reported at the time. The retail condo spans 18,000 square feet across four floors, according to Mezzo. Prada opened its flagship U.S. store there way back in 1996, which at that time was the luxury retailer’s largest store in the world. Saffati and spokespeople for RFR and JSRE did not immediately respond to requests for comment. RFR Holding recently created RFR US, an investment firm that will be helmed by Rosen’s sons, Gaby Rosen and Charlie Rosen and focus on new office and high-end retail assets. But RFR Holding has appeared to have fallen into tougher times lately with the sale of 281 Park Avenue South, best known as the old stomping grounds of fake heiress Anna Delvey. The firm offloaded the property in July for $81.5 million, compared to the $135 million it was originally listed for. bullets: RFR Holding acquires retail condo at 841 Madison Ave. from JSRE/Safra/Status for $57M.

stories.summary: RFR Holding, led by Aby Rosen and Michael Fuchs, acquired a retail condominium at 841 Madison Avenue occupied by Prada for $57 million, up from a $51 million sale in 2010. The transaction reflects renewed demand for high-end retail on Madison Avenue, with broker commentary highlighting the corridor's recovery and strong luxury tenant interest.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily relevance. However, sustained investment in Manhattan luxury retail (especially upper Madison Avenue) implies robust high-income tenant base and strong service-sector employment, which underpin demand for premium rental apartments in adjacent Upper East Side submarkets; retail recovery also suggests broader Manhattan economic recovery.

stories.title: Roadway Moving, Contenur Take Combined 231K SF at Innovo’s 28-90 Review Avenue
stories.excerpt: Innovo Property Group signed expansive leases for two industrial tenants in one of the company’s developments in Long Island City, Queens. In the largest of the two deals, Roadway Moving, a full-service moving and storage company, took 117,000 square feet on the first floor of Innovo’s 28-90 Review Avenue, also known as the Review Avenue Complex. Meanwhile, Spanish garbage container manufacturer Contenur leased 114,000 square feet on the second floor of the property, according to the landlord. Innovo did not immediately provide the asking rent or the lengths of the leases, but the average asking rent for industrial space in Queens was $27.50 per square foot in the second quarter of 2026, according to a report from Cushman & Wakefield. Pinnacle Realty’s David Junik, George Margaronis, Paul Bralower and Brendan Burke represented Innovo in the deals, while Ariel Castellanos and Daniel Tack, also from Pinnacle, negotiated on behalf of Roadway Moving. Frank Rao of New York Commercial Realty Group represented Contenur. Rao and spokespeople for Innovo and Pinnacle did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The deals, first reported by Bisnow, follow two other deals signed in May at the six-story industrial development, located near where the Gowanus Canal flows into Newtown Creek. Edge Auto Rental took 78,000 square feet on the first floor and 1-800-GOT-JUNK? leased 41,000 square feet on the first and third floors. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Roadway Moving leases 117K SF first floor; Contenur (Spanish garbage manufacturer) leases 114K SF second floor.
231K SF combined leases at Innovo's 28-90 Review Avenue, Long Island City, Queens.
Q2 2026 industrial asking rent: $27.50/SF in Queens; strong logistics/industrial demand.
stories.summary: Innovo Property Group signed two industrial leases totaling 231,000 square feet at its Review Avenue Complex in Long Island City, Queens: Roadway Moving took 117,000 SF on the first floor, and Spanish container manufacturer Contenur leased 114,000 SF on the second floor. The average asking rent for industrial space in Queens was $27.50 per square foot in Q2 2026.
stories.impact: Strong industrial leasing in Long Island City reflects sustained e-commerce and logistics demand, underpinning rents and asset values in Queens. As industrial space tightens, logistics tenants compete with multifamily developers for waterfront and near-waterfront sites in LIC; high industrial rents ($27.50/SF) may elevate land basis and development costs for competing multifamily projects in the neighborhood, compressing margins or pushing density requirements higher.
